# Remove blemishes

- Route: `/tools/remove-blemishes`
- Kind: `tool`
- Category: `photo`
- Slug: `remove-blemishes`

## Summary

Paint over spots, press Heal, and let an inpainting model on our GPU fill them from the surrounding skin. (Photo editing)

## Details

The Heal panel in Aperture is the one tool on this page that uses a model: you paint over each spot with the Spot brush, press Heal, and the painted mask plus the current image are sent to our own GPU server where LaMa inpainting reconstructs the covered pixels from what surrounds them. One press, with any number of spots marked, is one AI operation; it is refunded if the job fails, and in a saved project an identical repeat of the same mask on the same base is served from cache for free. The healed image becomes the new base that every later adjustment layer, mask and export starts from, while your original file is never modified. Skin, sensor dust, a stray hair on a backdrop and small signs all heal the same way.
### What it does
- Paints a spot mask with a hardness-80 brush at any size; dots and short strokes both work, and Clear spots empties the mask before you press Heal.
- Sends the mask with the current image to our GPU, where the LaMa inpainting model fills each masked region from the surrounding texture, in one job for all spots marked.
- Charges one AI operation per Heal press regardless of how many spots were marked, refunds it when the job fails, and returns a cached result at no charge for an identical repeat in a saved project.
- Makes the healed result the new base for the stack, so sharpening, color and masks applied later see clean skin, and the history panel can step back to before the heal.
- Leaves the original file untouched: the export renders the healed base at full resolution and writes a new file named with the (retouched) suffix.
### How to use it
1. Drop the photo: The Heal panel opens with the Spot brush active. Zoom in so each blemish is a few dozen screen pixels wide.
2. Mark the spots: Click or drag over each blemish with a brush slightly larger than the spot. The panel counts Spots marked as you go.
3. Press Heal: The mask is uploaded with the image and the job runs on our GPU; it can take up to a minute. Heals applied counts up when it returns.
4. Continue editing and export: Add more passes if needed, then adjust tone, sharpen and export. Undo or the history panel reverts a heal.
### Supported formats
- Input: JPG, PNG, WebP, GIF, HEIC, HEIF, AVIF, TIFF, BMP
- Output: JPG, PNG, WebP, AVIF, TIFF
- The heal mask must match the size of the current base; the editor builds it at that size automatically.
- Each Heal press is one AI operation; exports are everyday operations. Daily allowances are on the pricing page.
### Technical details
- The brush paints a raster in the geometry-corrected space you see and maps every stroke back through the crop, perspective, flips and rotation to source pixel coordinates, so the mask matches the base pixels even on a straightened, cropped photo. Each stroke is stamped with hardness 80 and flow 100; the uploaded mask is white where the alpha exceeds 0.05 and black elsewhere, at the size of the current base.
- A Heal press is one job: in a saved project it is POST /api/photo/projects/:id/heal with the mask and the current base hash; signed out it is the stateless /api/photo/heal route with the photo and mask uploaded for that job only. The server runs the LaMa model on the current base and stores the result as a new base whose name is the SHA-256 of the previous base hash and the mask digest, so the same mask on the same base is recognized and returned from cache without another AI operation.
- The document records each heal as an entry with the mask reference and the new base reference; every renderer, the WebGL preview, the server export and the batch apply, starts from the latest base rather than the original. Removing the entry in history restores the previous base.
- Red-eye is a separate panel: click an eye, a small circular mask is placed (default radius 2 percent of the long side) and inside it the red channel is replaced by min(r, (g + b)/2), so a pupil at (200, 40, 40) becomes (40, 40, 40). It is ordinary per-pixel color math with no AI operation.
- Everything other than the heal itself follows the Aperture parity policy: the preview is drawn on your GPU (WebGL2) from a 1920 px copy, the exported file is rendered on our server from the original, here the healed base, at full resolution with the same formulas, and the two agree within a small documented tolerance of a few 8-bit levels at most, exact for grain. The healed pixels themselves are produced once, on the server, and the preview shows a proxy of that same result.
### When not to use it
Heal is for spots and small marks, not for removing a whole person or a large object: a mask covering a big area gives the model too little context and the fill turns blurry or repetitive, and the dedicated Remove object tool on Media Manipulator is built for that job. Do not use it to smooth skin texture overall; use noise reduction or a negative Texture value, which are free and reversible. Large skin areas with strong pattern, such as freckles, heal unevenly, so mark only the blemish and keep a small margin.
### Use cases
- Portrait skin cleanup: Mark pimples, small scars and stray hairs with a brush about 1.5 times the spot, press Heal once for the whole face.
- Sensor dust on skies: Zoom to 100 percent, dot every dust shadow, heal once, and the smooth sky gradient is rebuilt without banding.
- Product photos: Remove lint and fingerprints on a backdrop before cutting out the subject, so the edge is clean.
- Scanned prints: Paint over scratches and spots from the scan glass; thin lines heal well when the brush covers them with a small margin.
### FAQ
Q: Is each spot a separate AI operation?
A: No. One press of Heal is one AI operation however many spots you painted, which is why the panel counts spots and lets you mark everything first.
Q: What happens if healing fails?
A: Nothing changes in the photo, the panel says the heal did not finish, and the AI operation is refunded. You can press Heal again with the same mask.
Q: Can I heal a blemish on a photo I have straightened or cropped?
A: Yes. Strokes are painted on the corrected view and mapped back through the geometry to source coordinates, so the mask lands on the right pixels of the base.
Q: Does healing change the original file?
A: Never. The result is stored as a new base inside the project and the export writes a separate file with the (retouched) suffix. Removing the heal in history returns to the previous base.
Q: How big should the brush be?
A: Slightly larger than the spot, with a margin of a few pixels, so the model does not sample the edge of the blemish itself. Oversized masks on textured areas take longer to look natural.
Q: Is red-eye removal part of Heal?
A: It is its own panel and needs no AI. Clicking an eye places a small circular mask and sets red to the smaller of itself and the average of green and blue inside it.
